# GreatCMS — complete documentation

This file concatenates the public docs in source order, for agents that prefer one fetch.

---
title: The GreatCMS Content Standard
source: SPEC.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/spec
---

# The GreatCMS Content Standard — version 1

This document is the product. Everything else in this repository is an
implementation of it.

A site is managed by GreatCMS if it contains a schema file and reads content
from the paths described here. That is the entire integration surface. No
plugin, no SDK, no runtime dependency, no build hook. If you can read JSON and
YAML, you can consume a GreatCMS site — and if you can read only JSON, you can
still consume one, because the schema may be written as JSON too.

Reading this document should be enough to write a consumer in any language in
under half an hour. If it is not, that is a bug in this document.

---

## 1. Repository layout

```
your-site/
├── .cms/
│   ├── schema.yaml       # or schema.json — the content model
│   └── config.yaml       # or config.json — paths and publishing (optional)
├── content/
│   ├── cms/              # structured regions, written by the studio
│   │   ├── home.hero.json
│   │   └── home.body.json
│   └── blog/             # collection entries
│       └── my-post.md
└── public/media/         # uploads, committed alongside content
```

Directories are configurable in `.cms/config.yaml`; the ones above are defaults.
Nothing else in the repository is touched by the CMS, ever.

---

## 2. Concepts

**Region** — a named slice of a page under CMS control: `home.hero`,
`pricing.faq`. Everything not declared a region is ordinary code the CMS never
sees. This is the hybrid model: a page can have one managed region, or be
entirely managed, and both are the same mechanism.

**Block** — a reusable field set. A _blocks region_ holds an ordered list of
blocks the editor can add, remove, and reorder.

**Collection** — a folder of entries with a shared shape: a blog, case studies,
changelog. Entries are Markdown with YAML frontmatter by default.

---

## 3. `.cms/schema.yaml`

```yaml
version: 1

site:
  name: My Site # optional, shown in the studio

blocks: # optional
  hero:
    label: Hero
    fields:
      heading: { type: text, required: true, max: 80 }
      image: { type: image }

regions: # at least one region or collection is required
  home.hero: # ← the region id
    label: Home hero
    fields:
      heading: { type: text, required: true, max: 80 }
      subtitle: { type: text, default: Welcome }
    default: # region-level defaults beat field-level defaults
      heading: Hello

  home.body:
    type: blocks
    allow: [hero]
    min: 0
    max: 8

collections: # optional
  blog:
    path: content/blog
    format: markdown # or json
    body: content # which field becomes the Markdown body
    slug: title # which field derives the file name
    fields:
      title: { type: text, required: true }
      date: { type: date, required: true }
      content: { type: richtext }
```

**Region ids** match `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*(\.[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*)*$`. They are
used verbatim as file names, so this is enforced, not advisory.

**Block and collection names** match `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*$`.

A JSON Schema for this file ships at `@greatcms/spec/json-schema`, giving
autocomplete and inline validation in any editor that supports it.

---

## 4. Field types

Every field accepts `label`, `description`, and `required`.

| Type       | Extra keys                                      | Stored value                                            |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `text`     | `min`, `max`, `pattern`, `multiline`, `default` | string                                                  |
| `richtext` | `allow`, `default`                              | `{ "html": "…", "_ast": … }`                            |
| `number`   | `min`, `max`, `step`, `integer`, `default`      | number                                                  |
| `boolean`  | `default`                                       | boolean                                                 |
| `select`   | `options`, `multiple`, `default`                | string, or array if `multiple`                          |
| `date`     | `time`, `default`                               | ISO 8601 string                                         |
| `link`     | `default`                                       | `{ "href": "…", "label"?: "…", "external"?: bool }`     |
| `image`    | `alt`, `accept`, `default`                      | `{ "src": "…", "alt": "…", "width"?: n, "height"?: n }` |
| `file`     | `accept`, `default`                             | `{ "src": "…", "name"?: "…", "size"?: n }`              |
| `list`     | `of`, `min`, `max`                              | array of the `of` type                                  |
| `group`    | `fields`                                        | nested object                                           |

`options` for `select` is either `[a, b]` or `[{ value: a, label: A }]`.

### Rich text

Rich text is stored as **sanitized HTML** in `html`, so a consumer can print it
with no library at all. The editor's structured document is preserved in `_ast`
for lossless round-tripping. **Consumers should ignore `_ast`.** Any key
beginning with `_` is machinery and may be ignored by consumers.

### Images and accessibility

Uploads are committed alongside content, into `content.media`, and served from
`mediaUrlPrefix`. Names are content-addressed so identical bytes reuse a path
and edited bytes get a new one.

`alt` is required by default. A field may set `alt: decorative-allowed`, which
is the only way an empty `alt` validates — making an inaccessible image a
deliberate choice rather than an oversight. `width` and `height` are recorded on
upload so consumers can prevent layout shift.

---

## 5. Content files

### Single region → `<regions dir>/<region-id>.json`

```json
{
  "heading": "Publish from anywhere",
  "subtitle": "Content in Git, deploys on commit.",
  "_meta": { "updatedAt": "2026-08-12T18:00:00.000Z", "updatedBy": "ada", "version": 1 }
}
```

### Blocks region → same path, `blocks` array

```json
{
  "blocks": [
    { "_type": "hero", "heading": "Hybrid by default" },
    { "_type": "cta", "label": "Read the spec", "link": { "href": "/spec" } }
  ]
}
```

Each block carries `_type`, naming a block defined in the schema.

### Collection entry → `<collection path>/<slug>.md`

```markdown
---
title: Publish from anywhere
date: 2026-08-12
tags: [release, git]
---

Body text becomes the field named by the collection's `body` key.
```

Files are written with two-space JSON indentation, keys sorted alphabetically
with `_`-prefixed keys last, and a trailing newline — so diffs stay readable and
two tools writing the same content produce the same bytes.

---

## 6. Resolution rules (the important part)

A consumer resolves a region in three steps. Getting these right is what the
conformance kit checks.

1. **Start from defaults.** Collect `default` from each field. For a blocks
   region, the default is the region's `default` array, or `[]`.
2. **Apply the region's `default` object**, which overrides field-level defaults.
3. **Layer the stored file on top**, if it exists.

Merge rules:

- Objects merge **deeply**, key by key.
- Arrays are **replaced wholesale** — merging lists item-by-item produces
  results no author would predict.
- Within a blocks region, each stored block is merged over its block's field
  defaults, so a field added to a block later still renders.
- **A missing content file is not an error.** The region resolves to its
  defaults, so a site builds correctly before the CMS has ever run.
- **A missing schema file _is_ an error.** Defaults live in the schema, so a
  consumer that cannot find it should fail loudly rather than quietly render
  empty regions. The schema is part of the site, committed alongside the code —
  what a site never depends on is the _studio_: no network call, no database, no
  API key, and no running service at build or request time. Shut the studio down
  permanently and every site it managed keeps building from what is in Git.
- A stored key the schema does not define is left alone by consumers. Only the
  studio treats unknown keys as an error, so a rename surfaces during editing
  rather than silently dropping content.

---

## 7. `.cms/config.yaml`

Optional; these are the defaults.

```yaml
version: 1
content:
  regions: content/cms
  media: public/media
mediaUrlPrefix: /media
publish:
  branch: main
  draftBranchPrefix: cms/draft
  commitMessage: "content: update {summary}"
  dispatchEvent: null # optional repository_dispatch after publish
preview:
  urlTemplate: null # e.g. https://{branch}--site.pages.dev
```

Paths must be repository-relative and may not contain `..`.

---

## 8. Publishing

The studio writes content with the GitHub Git Data API as a **single atomic
commit** per publish — blob, tree, commit, ref update — so a region and its
images land together or not at all. The commit is the deploy trigger; whatever
CI the repository already had does the rest. `publish.dispatchEvent` fires a
`repository_dispatch` for pipelines that need an explicit nudge.

Consumers are unaffected by all of this. They read files.

---

## 8a. Form submissions

Git cannot hold a message someone typed on your site, so the studio accepts one
directly:

```html
<form method="POST" action="https://studio.example.com/f/{siteId}/contact">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required />

  <input type="hidden" name="_redirect" value="/thanks/" />
  <input type="hidden" name="_t" value="1755024000000" />

  <div class="trap" aria-hidden="true">
    <label for="company">Company</label>
    <input id="company" name="company" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off" />
  </div>

  <button>Send</button>
</form>
```

Reserved names, stripped before storage:

| Field       | Meaning                                                     |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `_redirect` | Where to send the visitor afterwards. Same-site paths only. |
| `_t`        | When the form was rendered, in epoch milliseconds.          |
| `company`   | Honeypot. Hide it visually _and_ from assistive technology. |

Everything else is stored as the submission. Spam is scored from the honeypot,
the time between render and submit, and link density — never a CAPTCHA, which
taxes every legitimate visitor to inconvenience a bot that solves them anyway.
Suspected spam is kept, not discarded, so nothing is lost silently.

---

## 9. Conformance

```bash
npx @greatcms/conformance fixtures        # path to the fixture site
npx @greatcms/conformance verify ./out    # ./out holds <region-id>.json dumps
```

Point your reader at the fixture site, dump each resolved region as
`<region-id>.json` into a directory, and run `verify`. The fixture deliberately
includes a region with no content file, a region edited before a field was
added, a blocks region with a block missing a defaulted field, and a decorative
image with empty alt text — the four cases naive implementations get wrong.

A reference reader in Python (stdlib + PyYAML, ~120 lines) lives at
`examples/reader-python/read.py` and passes the suite. It is the shortest honest
answer to "how hard is this to integrate?".

---

## 10. Versioning

`version: 1` in both files. A consumer that sees a higher major version it does
not recognize should refuse rather than guess. New field types and optional keys
may be added within version 1; anything that changes how existing content
resolves requires a version bump and a documented migration.


---
title: GreatCMS Overview
source: README.md
url: https://greatcms.dev/
---

# thegreatcms

A Git-backed CMS for sites that shouldn't need one at runtime.

You pick which parts of a page it manages — a hero here, a feature list there,
an entire blog, or the whole site. Everything else stays hand-written code the
CMS never sees. Publishing writes files to your repository; the commit triggers
whatever deploy pipeline you already had. One studio manages many websites and
collects the things Git can't hold — form submissions, comments — into a single
inbox.

**It is not a framework plugin.** The integration surface is a schema file and
some JSON. Astro, Hugo, Eleventy, Next, Jekyll, Laravel, or a hand-rolled Go
generator all consume it the same way, in whatever language they're written in.

Read [SPEC.md](./SPEC.md) — that document is the actual product.

---

## Status

Milestone 4 of 5 (M3 and M4 both done). The standard is proven from two languages, the studio edits
and publishes real content to a real repository, and form submissions from any
site land in one inbox.

|                         |                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ✅ **M0** Foundation    | pnpm + Turborepo, oxlint + oxfmt (Rust), tsdown/Rolldown, Vitest             |
| ✅ **M1** The standard  | `@greatcms/spec`, conformance kit, Node reader, Astro example, Python reader |
| ✅ **M2** Studio        | Auth, multi-site registry, schema-generated editor, atomic publishes         |
| ✅ **M3** Preview       | Draft branch + your own CI, iframed                                          |
| ⬜ **M4** Dynamic layer | Forms, comments, inbox, email                                                |
| 🔄 **M5** Hardening     | a11y gates, perf budgets, CLI, agent docs                                    |

## What's here

```
apps/studio/            The CMS: sign in, connect repos, edit regions, publish
apps/docs/              The website — landing page and docs, managed by GreatCMS itself
packages/cli/           `greatcms preview` and `doctor` — the local half
packages/spec/          The standard: schema parsing, validation, resolution rules
packages/git/           Atomic multi-file commits via the GitHub Git Data API
packages/conformance/   Fixtures + verifier that prove a tool reads it correctly
packages/reader/        Build-time reader for any JS framework
examples/site-astro/    A real Astro site: managed regions beside hand-written markup
examples/reader-python/ The same standard, implemented in ~120 lines of Python
```

## Try it

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm test
```

Run the studio:

```bash
pnpm --filter @greatcms/studio build
STUDIO_PASSWORD='something long' pnpm --filter @greatcms/studio start
# http://localhost:8787
```

Connect a repository containing a `.cms/schema.yaml` and a token with
`contents: write`, and it builds the editor from your schema. Point any site's
contact form at `https://your-studio/f/{siteId}/contact` and the messages arrive
in the inbox — set `RESEND_API_KEY`, `NOTIFY_FROM`, and `NOTIFY_TO` to be emailed
about them too. Or run it as a
container — `apps/studio/Dockerfile`, one process, one SQLite file, one volume.

Then look at the example site:

```bash
pnpm --filter @greatcms/example-site-astro dev     # http://localhost:4321
```

The home page shows a managed hero next to a hand-written section — both end up
in the same static HTML. The about page renders from schema defaults, because
nobody has ever edited it.

## Setting up a site

```bash
npx greatcms init
```

It detects what you build with — Astro, Next, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Eleventy, Hugo,
Jekyll, or nothing in particular — and puts content where that generator already
looks for it: `data/cms` for Hugo, `_data/cms` for Eleventy and Jekyll,
`src/content/cms` for Astro. Then it asks what you want managed (one hero, a
landing page with reorderable blocks, a blog, or nothing yet), writes a
commented `.cms/schema.yaml` and `.cms/config.yaml` with the editor's
`$schema` line for autocomplete, and prints the snippet for reading your first
region **in your framework's own syntax**.

`--yes` takes every default; `--framework`, `--template`, `--name`, `--dir`, and
`--branch` override individually, so it scripts as well as it prompts. It
refuses to overwrite an existing setup without `--force`.

## Two kinds of site

**A folder on this machine.** Point the studio at a checkout and it reads and
writes the working copy directly — no token, no network, no push. Publishing
writes the files and commits them if the folder is a Git repository. Give it your
dev server's URL and the editor shows **your real components**, from your own
build, updating as soon as your dev server reloads.

**A GitHub repository.** Publishing commits over the API and your pipeline
deploys it, as below.

The studio needs exactly seven operations from a repository, and nothing about
them is specific to GitHub — which is why a folder works without a second code
path through the editor, the validation, or the publish.

## Publishing: straight to the branch, or as a pull request

Chosen per site when you connect it.

**Direct** commits to your publish branch. Fastest path from edit to live.

**Pull request** commits to a draft branch and opens a PR against it, so a
content change gets the same review, CI preview build, and revert-to-roll-back
that a code change does. Saving again updates the open pull request rather than
opening a second one.

Pull request titles are generated **from the actual field diff**:

> Update heading in Home hero on Example

with a table of every changed field in the body. That is the default, it needs
no model, and it is always accurate.

A site can opt in to having a model write the title instead. Point the studio at
any OpenAI-compatible endpoint and it works — Groq, Google's Gemini, Cloudflare
Workers AI, Mistral, or a local Ollama:

```bash
AI_BASE_URL=https://api.groq.com/openai/v1 AI_API_KEY=... AI_MODEL=llama-3.3-70b-versatile
```

Two things hold regardless: **publishing never waits on a model** — the call is
time-boxed and every failure falls back to the generated title — and the PR body
stays machine-generated, because a reviewer needs the change list to be true
rather than fluent. It is off by default per site, since it sends your content to
a third party.

## Images

Upload one in the editor and it is committed **in the same commit** as the
content that points at it. That is what the hand-built Git tree was for: if the
picture and the JSON referencing it landed separately, every deploy in between
would build a page with a broken image.

Width and height are read from the file's own header — no dependency, no
trusting the browser — so the stored value carries the intrinsic size and pages
do not reflow as images load. Files are content-addressed
(`hero-shot-a1b2c3d4.png`), so re-uploading identical bytes reuses the path
while an edited image gets a fresh URL that busts any cache holding the old one.

SVG is deliberately not accepted: it is a script-bearing document, and an editor
uploading one would be a stored-XSS vector on the published site. Alt text stays
required — uploading does not bypass validation.

## Previewing a draft

Three ways, at three speeds. None of them runs your code on our server.

**As you type.** The editor has a live preview pane that renders the content
currently in the form — before any save, commit, or branch. It updates while you
type, flags an image with no alt text where you will actually see it, and needs
nothing from your site. The layout is the studio's, not yours: it shows the
content, honestly labelled as such. Without JavaScript it becomes a button that
renders the same preview in a new tab.

The other two build your real site.

**Your CI builds it.** "Save draft & preview" commits to `cms/draft-<region>`;
set `preview.urlTemplate` in `.cms/config.yaml` and the studio iframes the
resulting URL.

**Or your own dev server builds it:**

```bash
npx greatcms preview --branch cms/draft-home.hero --run "npm run dev"
```

That overlays the draft's content files onto your working copy, starts your dev
server, and restores the working copy exactly when you stop it — including
deleting files that did not exist before. It refuses to run on top of
uncommitted content changes, and refuses any draft branch carrying changes
outside your content directories, because a draft is content, not code.

`npx greatcms doctor` prints what a repository's setup looks like: regions,
where each one's file lives, and which are still rendering schema defaults.

## Proofs, not claims

Each of these is an automated test, not a bullet point in a pitch:

**It works in another language.** A Python reader written from `SPEC.md` alone
passes the same conformance suite:

```bash
python3 examples/reader-python/read.py packages/conformance/fixtures /tmp/out
node packages/conformance/bin/greatcms-conformance.mjs verify /tmp/out
# conformance: PASS (5 regions)
```

**It ships nothing to the browser.** The built example site contains zero
`<script>` tags and weighs 34 KB across four pages — asserted in
`examples/site-astro/tests/a11y.test.ts`.

**It is accessible.** axe runs against every page of the example site _and_
every screen of the studio, every form control is labelled, and errors are
attached with `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` rather than colour alone.

**The admin degrades to plain HTML.** Every mutation is a form POST — including
adding, removing, and reordering blocks — so the studio is keyboard- and
screen-reader-navigable by construction rather than by patching ARIA onto custom
widgets. Rich text gets a visual editor built directly on **ProseMirror** (MIT,
no commercial tier), loaded only on screens that have a richtext field. It is an
enhancement over a real textarea: if the bundle never loads, you can still edit
and publish.

**A publish is one commit, or nothing.** Invalid content is refused before it
reaches the repository, and a branch that moved while you were editing gets a
409 rather than an overwrite.

**The studio never runs your code.** It reads your schema and writes content —
that is the whole interaction. Preview builds happen on your CI or your laptop,
which is also why one studio can manage an Astro site, a Hugo site, and a
Laravel site without carrying three toolchains.

**Form submissions need nothing on the site.** A plain HTML `<form>` posting to
the studio is the whole integration — no JavaScript, no third-party form
service, no per-site backend. Spam is scored with a honeypot, submission timing,
and a rate limit rather than a CAPTCHA, which is an accessibility tax paid by
every legitimate visitor to inconvenience a bot that solves them anyway.

**The awkward cases are covered.** The conformance fixture includes a region
with no content file, a region edited before a field was added to the schema, a
block missing a defaulted field, and a decorative image with empty alt text —
the four things naive implementations get wrong.

## Toolchain

Rust where a Rust tool exists, because build and check times are a feature:

| Job            | Tool                        | Why                                    |
| -------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Lint           | **oxlint** (oxc)            | Whole repo in ~1.4s, hundreds of rules |
| Format         | **oxfmt** (oxc)             | 65 files in ~0.7s, multi-threaded      |
| Library builds | **tsdown** (Rolldown + oxc) | ESM + declarations in ~2s per package  |
| Site builds    | **rolldown-vite**           | Astro build went 3.6s → 1.8s           |
| Task graph     | **Turborepo** (Rust)        | Content-hashed caching across packages |
| Tests          | **Vitest 4**                | Runs on the same Rolldown pipeline     |

## Design decisions worth knowing

**Content is JSON; prose is Markdown.** Every language parses JSON with no
dependencies, and every static site generator already has a Markdown pipeline.
Using one format for both would have fought one of those two facts.

**Rich text is sanitized HTML, with the editor AST beside it.** A consumer that
just wants to print a paragraph needs no library. `_ast` is there for anyone who
wants structural control, and is safe to ignore.

**Alt text is structurally required.** The only way to store an empty `alt` is a
field explicitly marked `alt: decorative-allowed`, which makes an inaccessible
image a deliberate act rather than an oversight.

**A missing content file is never an error.** It resolves to schema defaults, so
a site is correct before the CMS has ever been opened. A missing _schema_ file
is an error — failing loudly beats quietly rendering empty regions.

**Publishing is one atomic commit.** Blob → tree → commit → ref via the GitHub
Git Data API, so a region and its images land together or not at all. Repeated
`PUT /contents` calls can half-apply, and half-applied content is how `main`
stops building.

## The website

`apps/docs` is the project's site: a landing page and the documentation. Its
landing copy — the headline, the four claims, the closing note — is **managed by
GreatCMS**, stored as JSON in this repository and edited in the studio like any
other site. The layout around it is ordinary Astro the CMS has never seen.

The standard page renders `SPEC.md` directly, so the published standard and the
one the code implements cannot drift. It builds to 111 KB across nine pages,
ships no JavaScript, and holds the same axe and weight gates as everything else.

```bash
pnpm --filter @greatcms/docs dev
```

## For agents

The docs are published in a form a coding agent can consume in one fetch, since
"integrate from SPEC.md in half an hour" should be true for tools as well as
people:

```
/llms.txt        index and integration summary
/llms-full.txt   every document in one file
/docs.json       manifest, with agentEntrypoints and the integration steps
```

They are generated from `SPEC.md` and `README.md` by `pnpm run docs:build`, and
CI fails if they drift. [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md) covers working _on_ GreatCMS —
the invariants that are design decisions rather than implementation details.
